health-canada.definition: Canada's federal health department. It decides which medicines may be sold in Canada, checks their safety and acts against illegal sales.

food-and-drugs-act.definition: Canada's main federal law on food, medicines, cosmetics and medical devices. It says what counts as a drug and what may be sold and advertised.

food-and-drug-regulations.definition: The detailed rules made under Canada's Food and Drugs Act. They set out, for example, when a new drug may be sold and when it needs a DIN.

din.definition: An eight-digit number that Health Canada gives a drug it has authorised. It is printed on the label, and you can look it up in the Drug Product Database.

notice-of-compliance.definition: Health Canada's approval of a new drug. Nobody may sell or advertise a new drug in Canada until Health Canada has issued one.

prescription-drug-list.definition: Health Canada's list of medicinal ingredients. A medicine that contains an ingredient on the list is a prescription drug in Canada, unless the list says otherwise.

drug-product-database.definition: Health Canada's online list of drugs authorised in Canada, including ones that are no longer sold. You can search it by name or by DIN.

special-access-program.definition: A Health Canada route that lets a doctor ask for a drug not sold in Canada, for a patient with a serious or life-threatening condition when usual treatments have failed or do not suit. The company that makes the drug decides whether to supply it.

natural-health-product.definition: In Canada, a group of health products such as vitamins, minerals and herbal remedies. Each needs its own product licence. Nothing given by injection can be a natural health product.

canada-vigilance-program.definition: Health Canada's programme that collects and studies reports of side effects from medicines and other health products after they are on sale.

cbsa.definition: Canada's border agency. It can hold parcels and goods at the border and pass health products to Health Canada, which decides what happens to them.

type-i-recall.definition: Health Canada's most serious kind of recall. It is used when there is a reasonable chance that using the product will cause serious harm or death.

aliases: Canadian Centre for Ethics in Sport
sport-integrity-canada.definition: The body that runs the Canadian Anti-Doping Program. It used to be called the Canadian Centre for Ethics in Sport (CCES).

tga.definition: Australia's national medicines regulator. It decides which therapeutic goods may be supplied in Australia, checks their safety and acts against illegal supply and advertising.

therapeutic-goods-act.definition: Australia's main national law on medicines and other therapeutic goods. It covers who may import, make, supply and advertise them.

therapeutic-good.definition: In Australian law, a product for a health purpose, such as treating a disease or changing how the body works. Medicines are one kind of therapeutic good.

artg.definition: The TGA's public list of the therapeutic goods that can be legally supplied in Australia. A product must usually be on it before it is imported, supplied or advertised.

poisons-standard.definition: Australia's national list that sorts medicines and poisons into schedules, such as Schedule 4 for prescription-only medicines. The states and territories turn it into law.

schedule-4.definition: In Australia, the group of prescription-only medicines in the Poisons Standard. Being in Schedule 4 does not mean a medicine is approved or available.

appendix-d.definition: A part of Australia's Poisons Standard. One of its lists names medicines that must not be possessed without authority, such as a prescription, under the law of the state or territory.

s4d.definition: In New South Wales, prescription medicines on a special list that it is an offence to have without a prescription. Many performance and image enhancing drugs are on it.

special-access-scheme.definition: The TGA's routes that let a health practitioner supply an unapproved therapeutic good to one patient. Depending on the category, the practitioner tells the TGA or must get its approval first.

authorised-prescriber.definition: In Australia, a doctor whom the TGA allows to prescribe a particular unapproved medicine to a group of patients, usually with the support of an ethics committee or a specialist college.

personal-importation-scheme.definition: The Australian rules that let you import some unapproved medicines for yourself or close family, in limited amounts. A prescription-only medicine also needs a written authority from an Australian doctor.

infringement-notice.definition: A fine that a regulator such as the TGA can give for a breach of the law. If it is paid, the case does not go to court.

penalty-unit.definition: A fixed amount of money that Australian laws use to set fines. Each government sets its own value, and the value changes over time.

ahpra.definition: The Australian body that registers doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other health practitioners, and deals with concerns about them.

australian-border-force.definition: Australia's border agency. It can stop, seize and destroy goods at the border, including unlawful medicines that the TGA tells it about.

sport-integrity-australia.definition: The national body that runs anti-doping in Australia, set up by a law of 2020.

pieds.definition: Substances people use to build muscle, lose fat, change their looks or do better in sport, such as anabolic steroids, growth hormone and many peptides.

hpra.definition: Ireland's medicines regulator. It licenses medicines, inspects the companies that make or distribute them and collects reports of side effects. It used to be called the Irish Medicines Board.

hse-ireland.definition: Ireland's public health service. Its website explains where to get care and runs services such as needle exchanges.

medsafe.definition: New Zealand's medicines regulator, part of the Ministry of Health. It approves medicines, watches their safety and investigates illegal supply.

medicines-act-1981.definition: New Zealand's main law on medicines. It says who may sell, supply, import and advertise them, and makes it an offence to have a prescription medicine without a reasonable excuse.

section-29-nz.definition: The part of New Zealand's Medicines Act that lets an unapproved medicine be supplied to a doctor, nurse practitioner or pharmacist prescriber to treat a patient in their care.

carm.definition: New Zealand's centre for reports of side effects from medicines, part of the New Zealand Pharmacovigilance Centre at the University of Otago. Reports are made online through Medsafe's website.

sport-integrity-commission-nz.term: Sport Integrity Commission Te Kahu Raunui
sport-integrity-commission-nz.definition: The body that runs anti-doping in New Zealand. It took over from Drug Free Sport New Zealand on 1 July 2024.

ethics-committee.definition: A group of doctors, other experts and members of the public that checks a study plan before it may start. It asks whether the study is useful and not too risky for the people in it.
